questions.stem: According to the photon model, how is the energy of a photon related to the light it belongs to?
options: It is proportional to the amplitude of the light
It is proportional to the frequency of the light
It is proportional to the intensity of the light
It is proportional to the wavelength of the light
questions.explanation: E = hf, so a photon's energy depends only on frequency. Intensity sets how many photons arrive each second, not the energy of each one, and energy is inversely proportional to wavelength.

questions.stem: What is the energy of a photon of frequency 6.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz? Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
questions.explanation: E = hf = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 6.0 × 10¹⁴ = 3.98 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Dividing h by f instead gives 1.11 × 10⁻⁴⁸ J, far too small for a visible photon.

questions.stem: What is the momentum of a photon of wavelength 450 nm? Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
options: 1.47 × 10⁻²⁷ kg m s⁻¹
2.98 × 10⁻⁴⁰ kg m s⁻¹
4.42 × 10⁻¹⁹ kg m s⁻¹
4.91 × 10⁻³⁶ kg m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: p = h/λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ / 450 × 10⁻⁹ = 1.47 × 10⁻²⁷ kg m s⁻¹. The value 4.42 × 10⁻¹⁹ is the photon's energy in joules, hc/λ, not its momentum.

questions.stem: A photon has an energy of 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. What is its wavelength? Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
questions.explanation: f = E/h = 4.83 × 10¹⁴ Hz, then λ = c/f = 6.2 × 10⁻⁷ m (622 nm, orange light), or in one step λ = hc/E. The value 4.8 × 10¹⁴ is the frequency, mistakenly given in metres.

questions.stem: A 5.0 mW laser emits light of wavelength 633 nm. About how many photons does it emit each second? Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
questions.explanation: Each photon carries hc/λ = 3.14 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, so the number per second is 5.0 × 10⁻³ / 3.14 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.6 × 10¹⁶. Leaving the power in milliwatts gives 1.6 × 10¹⁹, a thousand times too many.

questions.stem: Why does a perfectly reflecting solar sail receive a larger push from sunlight than an identical sail that absorbs all the light?
options: Absorbed photons transfer their momentum to heat, so they cannot push the sail
Reflection increases the number of photons striking the sail each second
Each reflected photon's momentum is reversed, so the change in momentum is doubled
Reflected photons gain energy from the sail, so they carry away much more momentum
questions.explanation: A photon carries momentum p = h/λ. If it is absorbed its momentum changes by p, but if it is reflected straight back its momentum changes by 2p, so the sail receives twice the impulse.

questions.stem: What is the photoelectric effect?
options: The emission of electrons from a metal surface when light of high enough frequency falls on it
The emission of light from a metal surface when electrons of high enough speed strike the surface
The heating of a metal surface when light of any frequency is absorbed by it
The flow of current through a metal when a potential difference is applied to it
questions.explanation: In the photoelectric effect, light of sufficiently high frequency ejects electrons from a metal surface. The reverse process, where fast electrons produce radiation from a target, is how X-rays are made.

questions.stem: Monochromatic light above the threshold frequency falls on a metal. The intensity of the light is doubled. What happens to the emitted electrons?
options: Twice as many are emitted each second, with twice the maximum kinetic energy
The same number are emitted each second, with the same maximum kinetic energy
Twice as many are emitted each second, with the same maximum kinetic energy
The same number are emitted each second, with twice the maximum kinetic energy
questions.explanation: Doubling the intensity doubles the number of photons arriving each second, so twice as many electrons are released. Each photon still has energy hf, so the maximum kinetic energy is unchanged.

questions.stem: What is the work function of a metal surface?
options: The energy of the photons that eject the fastest electrons
The minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the surface
The maximum kinetic energy of an electron emitted from the surface
The minimum frequency of light that can remove an electron from the surface
questions.explanation: The work function W is the least energy that must be supplied to free an electron from the surface. The minimum frequency is the threshold frequency f₀, related to it by W = hf₀.

questions.stem: A metal has a threshold frequency of 1.10 × 10¹⁵ Hz. What is its work function in electronvolts? Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
questions.explanation: W = hf₀ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 1.10 × 10¹⁵ = 7.29 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, and 7.29 × 10⁻¹⁹ / 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 4.56 eV. Quoting 7.29 forgets to convert from joules to electronvolts.

questions.stem: In a photoelectric experiment the photocurrent falls to zero when the stopping voltage reaches 0.85 V. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons? Use e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
questions.explanation: E_K max = eV_s = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 0.85 = 1.36 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, which is 0.85 eV. Dividing V_s by e gives 5.31 × 10¹⁸, which is not an energy at all.

questions.stem: Light of frequency 8.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz falls on a surface with a work function of 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons? Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
questions.explanation: E_K max = hf − W = 5.30 × 10⁻¹⁹ − 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 2.1 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. The value 5.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J is the photon energy before the work function is subtracted.

questions.stem: Ultraviolet light of wavelength 250 nm falls on a metal with a work function of 4.3 eV. What stopping voltage is needed to stop the photocurrent? Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
questions.explanation: hf = hc/λ = 7.96 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 4.97 eV, so E_K max = 4.97 − 4.3 = 0.67 eV and the stopping voltage is 0.67 V. Using 4.97 V forgets the work function; 9.27 V adds it instead of subtracting.

questions.stem: A graph of the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons (vertical axis) against frequency is a straight line. Extended back, where does it cut the vertical axis?
options: At f₀, the metal's threshold frequency
At zero, for every metal tested
At −W, minus the work function
At h, the value of Planck's constant
questions.explanation: E_K max = hf − W has the form y = mx + c, with gradient h and vertical intercept −W. The line crosses the frequency axis at the threshold frequency f₀, not the energy axis.

questions.stem: Graphs of maximum kinetic energy against frequency are drawn for two different metals on the same axes. How do the two lines compare?
options: They lie on top of each other, because h is the same
They are parallel, but cross the frequency axis at different points
They have different gradients but cross the frequency axis at the same point
They have different gradients and meet at the origin
questions.explanation: The gradient of each line is Planck's constant, the same for every metal, so the lines are parallel. Each metal has its own work function, so each line has its own threshold frequency and vertical intercept.

questions.stem: A student measures maximum kinetic energies of 1.30 × 10⁻¹⁹ J at 7.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz and 2.62 × 10⁻¹⁹ J at 9.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. What is the threshold frequency of the metal?
options: 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz
6.6 × 10¹⁴ Hz
2.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz
3.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz
questions.explanation: The gradient is (2.62 − 1.30) × 10⁻¹⁹ / 2.0 × 10¹⁴ = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. Then f₀ = 7.0 × 10¹⁴ − 1.30 × 10⁻¹⁹ / 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ = 7.0 × 10¹⁴ − 2.0 × 10¹⁴ = 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. The value 2.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz is only the shift back from the first point.

questions.stem: In a photoelectric experiment, how is the stopping voltage for a given frequency of light found?
options: The frequency is reduced until electrons are no longer emitted at all
The reverse potential difference is increased until the photocurrent just falls to zero
The light intensity is reduced until the photocurrent just falls to zero
The forward potential difference is increased until the photocurrent stops rising
questions.explanation: A reverse potential difference repels the emitted electrons; when even the fastest ones are stopped the current reaches zero, and eV_s = E_K max. Reducing frequency until emission stops finds the threshold frequency instead.

questions.stem: Which result of the photoelectric effect could the wave model of light NOT explain?
options: The number of electrons emitted depends on the metal's surface area
Below the threshold frequency no electrons are emitted, however intense the light
Brighter light above the threshold frequency releases more electrons each second
The emitted electrons have a range of kinetic energies up to a maximum
questions.explanation: In the wave model, energy arrives continuously, so intense enough light of any frequency should eventually free electrons. The existence of a threshold frequency shows energy arrives in packets of size hf.

questions.stem: How did Einstein explain the photoelectric effect?
options: Photons knock electrons out by colliding with them and bouncing off with lower frequency
Each photon gives all its energy to one electron, which spends some escaping and keeps the rest
Each electron absorbs energy from many photons until it has gathered enough to escape the surface
The light's electric field shakes the electrons harder as the light is made brighter
questions.explanation: Einstein applied conservation of energy to a single photon-electron interaction: hf = W + E_K max for the least tightly bound electrons. Electrons do not accumulate energy from several photons, which is why a threshold frequency exists.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the heated filament in a simple X-ray tube?
options: To absorb the X-rays that travel backwards
To slow the electrons before they strike the target
To produce the characteristic X-ray peaks
To release electrons by thermionic emission
questions.explanation: The filament is heated by a current so that electrons gain enough energy to leave it. These electrons are then accelerated by the large potential difference across the tube towards the target.

questions.stem: Why is an X-ray tube evacuated?
options: So the filament can be heated without needing an electric current
So the target stays cool while the electrons strike it
So the electrons do not collide with gas molecules on the way to the target
So the X-rays produced are not absorbed by air before they leave the glass tube
questions.explanation: Without a vacuum, electrons would collide with gas molecules, losing energy and ionising the gas, and would not reach the target at high speed. Air absorbs X-rays only weakly, so that is not the main reason.

questions.stem: Why must the target of an X-ray tube be cooled?
options: The filament radiates most of its heat directly onto the target
The potential difference drives a large current through the target
Most of the electrons' kinetic energy becomes heat in the target, not X-rays
The X-rays produced inside the target heat it strongly as they leave its surface
questions.explanation: Only a small fraction of the electrons' kinetic energy is emitted as X-ray photons; the rest heats the target. A high melting-point metal such as tungsten is used, often with a rotating anode or circulating oil to remove the heat.

questions.stem: Which sequence describes the main energy changes in an X-ray tube?
options: Heat in the filament to X-rays directly, with the potential difference adding light
Chemical energy in the target to electron kinetic energy, then X-rays
Electrical potential energy to electron kinetic energy, then mostly heat and some X-rays
Electron kinetic energy to electrical potential energy, then mostly X-rays and some heat
questions.explanation: The potential difference accelerates the electrons, converting electrical potential energy to kinetic energy. When they strike the target, most of that energy becomes heat and a small part is emitted as X-rays.

questions.stem: An X-ray tube operates with a potential difference of 40 kV. What is the maximum frequency of the X-rays produced? Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
options: 9.7 × 10¹⁸ Hz
6.0 × 10¹⁸ Hz
9.7 × 10¹⁵ Hz
questions.explanation: f_max = eΔV/h = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 4.0 × 10⁴ / 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ = 9.7 × 10¹⁸ Hz. Using 40 V instead of 40 kV gives 9.7 × 10¹⁵ Hz.

questions.stem: What is the shortest wavelength of the X-rays from a tube operating at 30 kV? Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
questions.explanation: The maximum frequency is eΔV/h = 7.24 × 10¹⁸ Hz, so the shortest wavelength is c/f_max = hc/(eΔV) = 4.1 × 10⁻¹¹ m. The value 7.2 × 10¹⁸ is the frequency, not a wavelength.

questions.stem: What produces the continuous range of frequencies (bremsstrahlung) in the spectrum from an X-ray tube?
options: X-ray photons being scattered back and forth inside the evacuated tube
Electrons decelerating in the target and losing different amounts of energy as photons
Electrons in the target's atoms dropping between fixed inner energy levels
Electrons leaving the filament with a range of different temperatures
questions.explanation: Bremsstrahlung, or braking radiation, comes from electrons slowing as they pass near target nuclei; each can lose any amount of energy up to its total, giving a continuous spread. Transitions between fixed inner levels produce the characteristic peaks instead.

questions.stem: Why does the X-ray spectrum from a tube have a sharp maximum frequency?
options: The target absorbs every X-ray photon above a certain frequency
The filament can only emit electrons below a certain kinetic energy
Photons above that frequency are cancelled out by destructive interference in the tube
An electron can give at most all of its kinetic energy, eΔV, to a single photon
questions.explanation: Each electron arrives with kinetic energy eΔV. The most energetic photon is made when one electron loses all that energy at once, so hf_max = eΔV.

questions.stem: What produces the high-intensity peaks at particular frequencies in an X-ray spectrum?
options: Electrons from outer levels of target atoms filling gaps left by ejected inner electrons
Electrons from the filament being stopped completely in a single collision
The potential difference across the tube rising and falling at fixed frequencies
Bremsstrahlung photons being reflected back from the walls of the tube
questions.explanation: An incoming electron can knock an inner electron out of a target atom. An electron from a higher level drops into the vacancy, emitting a photon whose energy equals the gap between the levels, so the peaks are characteristic of the target metal.

questions.stem: The potential difference across an X-ray tube is increased while the filament current stays the same. How does the spectrum change?
options: The maximum frequency rises, but the characteristic peaks stay at the same frequencies
The maximum frequency rises, and the characteristic peaks shift to higher frequencies
The maximum frequency stays the same, but the whole spectrum becomes more intense
The maximum frequency falls, and the characteristic peaks disappear
questions.explanation: f_max = eΔV/h, so a larger potential difference raises the maximum frequency and the overall output. The characteristic peaks depend only on the target's energy levels, so their frequencies do not change.

questions.stem: The filament current of an X-ray tube is increased while the tube voltage stays the same. What is the effect?
options: More electrons strike the target, so the X-ray intensity rises at every frequency
The electrons strike the target faster, so the maximum frequency rises
The characteristic peaks move to higher frequencies and become sharper
The X-rays become more penetrating, so their hardness increases
questions.explanation: A hotter filament emits more electrons each second, so more X-ray photons are produced, raising intensity without changing their energies. The electrons' speed, and so the maximum frequency and hardness, depend on the tube voltage.

questions.stem: Why do bones show up clearly on an X-ray image of an arm?
options: Bone emits its own X-rays when the beam passes through it
Soft tissue reflects X-rays back towards the X-ray tube
Bone makes the X-rays more penetrating as they pass through
Bone attenuates X-rays more strongly than the surrounding soft tissue
questions.explanation: X-rays are attenuated by scattering and absorption, and denser bone attenuates far more than soft tissue. Fewer X-rays reach the detector behind bone, giving the contrast that shows its outline.

questions.stem: A technician needs X-rays that can pass through a thick metal casting to check it for flaws. What should they change?
options: Cool the target more strongly to produce higher-frequency X-rays
Increase the tube voltage to produce harder, higher-frequency X-rays
Increase the filament current to produce harder, higher-frequency X-rays
Decrease the tube voltage to produce softer, longer-wavelength X-rays
questions.explanation: Penetrating power, or hardness, depends on photon energy, so higher-frequency X-rays are needed for dense metal. Photon energy is set by the tube voltage; the filament current changes only the intensity.

questions.stem: An X-ray photograph needs a minimum exposure of 0.40 s. The filament current is then increased so that the X-ray intensity doubles, with the same hardness. What is the new minimum exposure time?
questions.explanation: The film or detector needs a fixed amount of X-ray energy of that hardness, so exposure time is inversely proportional to intensity. Doubling the intensity halves the time to 0.20 s.

questions.stem: What does the de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p describe?
options: The wavelength associated with a moving particle, which depends on its momentum
The wavelength of the photon a particle emits when it is accelerated
The shortest wavelength of light that can eject an electron from a metal
The distance a particle travels before it collides with another particle
questions.explanation: De Broglie proposed that every moving particle has a wavelength h/p. The larger the momentum, the shorter the wavelength, which is why wave behaviour is noticeable only for very small particles.

questions.stem: What is the de Broglie wavelength of an electron moving at 3.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹? Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and electron mass 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
questions.explanation: p = mv = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × 3.0 × 10⁶ = 2.73 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹, so λ = h/p = 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Taking momentum as ½mv doubles the answer to 4.9 × 10⁻¹⁰ m; momentum is mv.

questions.stem: In the Davisson-Germer experiment, electrons were accelerated from rest through 54 V. What was their de Broglie wavelength? Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and electron mass 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
questions.explanation: E_K = eV = 8.64 × 10⁻¹⁸ J and p = √(2mE_K) = 3.97 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹, so λ = h/p = 1.67 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Leaving out the 2 in √(2mE_K) gives 2.36 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. The answer is close to the spacing of atoms in a crystal, which is why diffraction was seen.

questions.stem: Why is the wave behaviour of a cricket ball never observed?
options: Only particles moving close to the speed of light have a de Broglie wavelength
Its large momentum gives a wavelength far smaller than any gap it could pass through
It has no charge, so it cannot interact with its own matter wave
Its wavelength is so large that the interference fringes are too far apart to ever be found
questions.explanation: A 0.16 kg ball at 30 m s⁻¹ has λ = h/mv ≈ 1.4 × 10⁻³⁴ m, far smaller than any gap or atom. Diffraction is noticeable only when the wavelength is comparable to the size of the gap or obstacle.

questions.stem: What did the Davisson-Germer experiment show?
options: Light falling on a metal surface ejected electrons with a maximum kinetic energy
Electrons in atoms occupy discrete energy levels with fixed energies
Electrons scattered from the surface layers of a crystal formed a diffraction pattern
Electrons striking a metal target produced a continuous X-ray spectrum
questions.explanation: Davisson and Germer fired electrons at a nickel crystal and found strong scattering at particular angles, like the orders of a diffraction grating. This confirmed that electrons have a wavelength given by h/p.

questions.stem: Electrons pass through a double slit and form an interference pattern. The electrons are then accelerated to a higher speed. How does the pattern change?
options: The pattern disappears, because fast electrons travel in straight lines
The bright bands move closer together, because the electrons' wavelength is shorter
The bright bands move further apart, because the electrons' wavelength is longer
The bright bands stay the same, because the slits have not changed
questions.explanation: Greater speed means greater momentum, so λ = h/p is shorter. As with light, a shorter wavelength gives smaller fringe spacing, so the bands crowd together.

questions.stem: A proton and an electron move at the same speed. How does the proton's de Broglie wavelength compare with the electron's?
options: About 1800 times longer, because a more massive particle has a longer matter wave
The same, because the two particles are moving at the same speed
The same, because the two particles carry the same size of charge
About 1800 times shorter, because its mass and momentum are that much larger
questions.explanation: At equal speed, λ = h/mv is inversely proportional to mass. The proton is about 1836 times more massive than the electron, so its wavelength is about that many times shorter.
